newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela seen heading African drive for peace.
newsitem.headline: Mandela seen heading African drive for peace.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela's surprise bid for peace in Zaire could be the start of a renewed African effort to seize the initiative in resolving Africa's conflicts, diplomats and analysts said.
But they cautioned that neither South Africa nor Africa as a whole had the experience or the resources to go it alone.
Mandela gave a hint of the thinking that might have caused his unilateral effort to shepherd the Zairean combatants towards peace when he told Reuters recently:
"Africa would like to feel that they are handling things themselves...not acting in response to suggestions that come from outside the continent."
Three Western diplomats who agreed to discuss the issue on condition of anonymity said Mandela could help to break what they saw as a pattern of diplomatic dependence.
"It's something we welcome enormously. Mr Mandela could be the individual who makes the difference between failure and success in often very complicated situations," said one.

Another said Mandela's decision to launch secret talks to try to bring the warring sides in Zaire together with only modest hope of success could help break a mould of diplomatic caution that had allowed some conflicts to run out of control.

"Africa needs this sort of honest and courageous action just to get out of the endless and fruitless cycle of meetings of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) and the United Nations," he said.

Mandela's current initiative, which political sources say is heavily influenced by Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, has been more sophisticated than his emotional and abortive bid to resolve the crisis in Nigeria.
He retreated bruised in November 1995 from his unsuccessful attempt to force the West and the Commonwealth to use sanctions to starve oil-rich Nigeria's military leader Sani Abacha into submission.
Since then he has exercised his clout through the continent's and world's key institutions, consulting and informing SADC, the OAU and the United Nations on virtually every move.
Now, however, he seems ready again to exert a little more force in favour of peace on a continent that is fast exhausting the patience and purses of its Western benefactors.
One presidential adviser told Reuters that Mandela was anxious to bring the initiative for conflict resolution and control of the process back to the African continent.

"The president sometimes feels that Western countries do not always act in the best interests of Africa, but rather in their own best interests when they try to guide countries in Africa to a solution," the adviser said.
An official in Mandela's government said: "There is a perception that the United States and Europe are often self-serving in their efforts to help Africa."

Africa's major challenge in resolving its own problems is likely to be that it does not have the resources to go beyond the political peace-making of the current initiative into the expensive phase of food aid and aid delivery.

"There is a capacity in South Africa that could be used to help out in the region, but these things are hellish expensive and they have not been budgeted for," said Stellenbosch University political analyst Willem Breytenbach.
"Preventive diplomacy is cheap and effective."
Some analysts say preventive diplomacy could also be a safer arena for South Africa's inexperienced leaders.
"There is a growing interest in South Africa in trying to influence the foreign affairs of the region. But South Africa is very new to the game and the lack of experience shows.
"They bring the enormous prestige of President Mandela and only a modest capability to the problem," said one diplomat.
He cited Mandela's decision nearly two weeks ago to announce the impending peace bid, despite a decision by all the players to keep it a secret, as a blunder that could have torpedoed the initiative.
